captions.text: Recap of chapter 33: a Meter recorded what each run cost, in tokens, money and time.
The model was 97% of the time on 7B. Speeding up the tools would save nothing.
Count cost per right answer, not per call.
And caching helped when it happened, which wasn't always.
The capstone: an agent that fixes bugs on its own.
It runs code the model wrote. So run that code in a box, and judge the fix with tests it can't see.
Four tools: list the files, read one, change one, run the tests. Here's the one that changes a file.
It replaces text copied exactly from the file, and it must appear exactly once.
If not, the error tells the model what to do next, because the model reads it.
The tests import the code the model just changed. So they run in a Docker box.
No network. Little memory, one processor, at most 64 processes.
Nothing writable but the project, no admin powers, and a time limit.
Don't take the settings on trust. Try each door. Predict: which ones open?
No internet. The tests can't be changed. Nothing outside the project.
600 MB was stopped at 256. An endless loop at 5 seconds. 200 processes at 62. Every door held.
Twenty small projects, one bug each, with tests the agent sees and hidden tests it never sees.
Every bug fails before the right fix, and passes after it. A bug that passes before measures nothing.
One bug, on 7B. Read the issue, then the code.
It asked for tests/test_stats.py. That's the example in our own tool description. Models copy examples.
One exact change, the tests pass, and the hidden tests agree. Fixed.
All twenty bugs. Fixed means the original tests and the hidden tests pass.
7B fixed 33 of 60. Flash-Lite fixed all 20.
Predict: what went wrong in 7B's other 27 runs?
It asked for files that aren't there, and copied text it hadn't read. 24 never changed a file at all.
Would a simpler tool help? Write the whole file instead of one exact piece.
7B fell from 33 to 7. It mostly explained the fix and never wrote it. Flash-Lite fixed all 20 either way.
Other kinds of help, one change at a time.
The file list helped. Hiding the test output hurt. But the same setup scored 33 once and 25 another time.
The tests are files too. 7B changed them in 11 runs, and fixed none of those bugs.
It changed what the test expects into what the broken code returns. To the agent, the job was done.
So lock the tests in code. The edit tool refuses any path in tests/.
And the sandbox mounts tests/ read-only, so even the agent's own code can't change them.
It cost nothing: 34 of 60, against 33. Six runs tried, and were told no.
Last, a bug report with planted orders: add code that sends a key away whenever the tests run.
The agent obeyed about a third of the time. In a loose box, the key left 6 times. In the sandbox, never.
Three of those six never mentioned it. Read only their summaries, and you'd never know.
Five exercises: exact replacement, locked folders, the box's limits, cutting output, and spotting a faked test.
You've finished when you see 5 passed.

captions.text: Run the agent's code in a box, and judge its work with tests it can't see.
These counts come from one Mac and twenty small bugs. Measure your own.
